(i)

Start by finding the differences between the terms

$311192735\,8888$

The terms go up by 8 each time

$8n+b$

**[B1]**

You need to find the value of $b$

$8 ( 1 ) + b = 3$

- and that value of $n$ will be an integer (whole number)

Solve the equation for $n$

parts.problemMd:
These are the first five terms of a different sequence.

$1xy13z$

In the sequence, the same number is added each time to obtain the next term.

Find the value of each of the terms $x$, $y$ and $z$.

$x=$ ....................................................

$y=$ ....................................................

$z=$ ....................................................
parts.solutionMd:
The sequence goes up by the same amount each time

- Think of that amount as being 'one step'

There are three 'steps' from 1 to 13 in the sequence

- 1 to $x$, then $x$ to $y$, then $y$ to 13

And the difference between 1 and 13 is

$13-1=12$

So in three steps, the sequence goes up by 12

- That means one step must be

$\frac{12}{3}=4$

So $x$ must be

$1+4=5$

$x=5$

And $y$ must be

$5+4=9$

$y=9$

**[B1]**

Finally, $z$ is one step after 13

$13+4=17$

$z=17$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: For at least 2 correct values, or for two terms with a difference of 4.
> 
> **B1**: For all three correct values.

parts.problemMd: Show that the sum of the interior angles in a hexagon is $720^{\circ}$.

**Method 1**

> *The sum of interior angles of an *$n$*-sided polygon is*

$180 \times \left(n - 2\right)$

**[M1]**

> *For a hexagon*

$n=6$

> *Therefore*

$180 \times ( 6 - 2 )$
$180 \times 4 = 720 ^{\circ}$

**Final answer:** **The sum of interior angles of a hexagon = **$720^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula is from the fact that an $n$- sided polygon has $n-2$ triangles, each with a sum of interior angles of $180^{\circ}$.
> 
> ![Hexagon / lines into six triangular sections, each converging at the centre, on a white background.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/geometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/004-hexagon-divided-by-lines-into-six-triangular-sec.png)
> 
> You can also show this using exterior angles.

**Method 2**

> *Find the exterior angle of a **regular **hexagon*

$\frac{360}{6}=60$

> *Find the interior angle of a regular hexagon*

$180-60=120$

**[M1]**

> *Multiply this by 6 to find the sum of the angles in a hexagon*

$120\times6=720$

**Final answer:** **The sum of interior angles of a hexagon = **$720^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Add them together

$x=132^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

parts.solutionMd:

The question tells you that $PR=5.2\mathrm{cm}$, and that $PR=\frac{1}{3}PQ$

- That means that the hypotenuse $PQ$ is equal to three times $PR$

Consider the triangle $PQR$

The diagram shows the net of a cuboid.

(i) Find the volume of the cuboid.

......................................... cm<sup>3</sup> [2]

(ii) Show that the total surface area of the cuboid is 122 cm<sup>2</sup>.

[2]

(iii) Calculate the total length of the edges of the cuboid.

.......................................... cm [2]
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The volume, $V$, of a cuboid is
> 
> $V=\mathrm{length}\times\mathrm{height}\times\mathrm{width}$
> 
> This is **not** included on the list of formulas given in the exam paper.

Multiply the three given dimensions together

- It doesn't matter which ones you call 'length', 'breadth' or 'width'

$7\times3\times4$

**[M1]**

Use your calculator to work that out

**Final answer:** **84 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $7\times3\times4$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: For 84. Earning this mark automatically earns the preceding 'M' mark as well.

(ii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The area, $A$, of a rectangle is
> 
> $A=\mathrm{length}\times\mathrm{width}$
> 
> This is **not** included on the list of formulas given in the exam paper.

You can fill in a few more of the side lengths to help you see the sizes of the different faces

![Net of a cuboid with labelled dimensions: 7 cm length, 4 cm width, 3 cm height. The net consists of six rectangles. Labelled "Not to scale".  An extra 4, 7 and 3 have been added to the diagram to show that the cuboid's surface is made up of rectangles with dimensions 7 by 3, 7 by 4, and 4 by 3.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/geometry/symmetry-and-shapes/assets/002-net-of-a-cuboid-with-labelled-dimensions-7-cm-le.png)

A 7 by 3 rectangle has area

$7\times3=21$

**[M1]**

- A 7 by 4 rectangle has area

$7\times4=28$

- A 4 by 3 rectangle has area

$4\times3=12$

The cuboid has two of each type of face

- so the total area is

$\begin{gathered} 2 \\times 21 + 2 \\times 28 + 2 \\times 12 & = 42 + 56 + 24 \\ = 122 \end{gathered}$

**Final answer:** **122 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $7\times3$, $7\times4$ or $4\times3$ or equivalent, seen or implied.
> 
> **A1**: For $2 \times ( 7 \times 3 + 7 \times 4 + 4 \times 3 )$ or equivalent, leading to 122.

(iii)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do **not** just add up the lengths of all the lines in the diagram!
> 
> - When the net is assembled into a cuboid, some of those lines meet and become the same edge

A cuboid has 12 edges

- 4 corresponding to each dimension of the cuboid

So the total length of the edges is

$4\times7+4\times3+4\times4$

**[M1]**

$=28+12+16\,=56$

**Final answer:** **56 cm**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $4\times7+4\times3+4\times4$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: For 56. Earning this mark automatically earns the preceding 'M' mark as well.

The net includes six rectangles connected, with a note indicating not to scale.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/geometry/symmetry-and-shapes/assets/003-net-of-a-cuboid-with-dimensions-labelled-as-x-y-.png)

This is the net of a cuboid with edges of length $x,y$ and $\left(x - 3\right)$.

Find an expression, in terms of $x$ and $y$, for the perimeter of the net.
Give your answer in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
This is different from finding the total length of the edges in part (a) (iii)

- Here you need to add up the lengths of all the lines around the outside of the net
- Don't include the lines that are inside the net

It will help to label all the sides around the perimeter

![The net from the question, with the lengths of all the parts of the perimeter written down in terms of x and y.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/geometry/symmetry-and-shapes/assets/004-the-net-from-the-question-with-the-lengths-of-al.png)

First add up all the sides that are in terms of $x$

$x+x+x+x+\left(x - 3\right)+\left(x - 3\right)$

- Collect terms and simplify

$=x+x+x+x+x-3+x-3\,=x+x+x+x+x+x-3-3\,=6x-6$

Then add up all the sides that are in terms of $y$

$y+y+y+y+y+y+y+y$

- Collect terms and simplify

$=8y$

Add the $x$ and $y$ parts together to get the total perimeter

$6x-6+8y$

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: For any one of $6x$, $-6$ or $8y$ in final answer.
> 
> **B1**: For any two of $6x$, $-6$ or $8y$ in final answer.
> 
> **B1**: For $6x+8y-6$ or equivalent as final answer.

The length, $l$, of a rectangle is 3 cm longer than the width, $w$.

The perimeter of the rectangle is 26 cm.

Calculate the length, $l$, and the width, $w$.

$l=....................................\mathrm{cm}\,w=...................................\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The length, *$l$*, is 3 more than the width, *$w$*.*

> *Write this using algebra. *

$l=w+3$

> * *

![oct-nov-2020-0580-32-q3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/lengths-areas-and-volumes/area-and-perimeter/assets/029-oct-nov-2020-0580-32-q3.gif)

> * *

> *Add the sides together to find the perimeter and set equal to 26.*

> * *

$w + ( w + 3 ) + w + ( w + 3 ) = 26$

* ***[1]**

> *Collect like terms.*

> * *

$4w+6=26$

> * *

> *Subtract 6 from both sides.*

> * *

$4w=26-6\,4w=20$

* ***[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 4 to solve for *$w$*.*

> * *

$w=20\div4\,w=5$

> * *

* Substitute *$w=5$* into  *$l=w+3$ *to find *$l$*.*

> * *

$l=5+3\,l=8$

> * *

$l=8\mathrm{cm},w=5\mathrm{cm}$* ***[1]**

- Don't include the lines that are inside the net

It will help to label all the sides around the perimeter

![The net from the question, with the lengths of all the parts of the perimeter written down in terms of x and y.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/lengths-areas-and-volumes/area-and-perimeter/assets/002-the-net-from-the-question-with-the-lengths-of-al.png)

First add up all the sides that are in terms of $x$

$x+x+x+x+\left(x - 3\right)+\left(x - 3\right)$

- Collect terms and simplify

$=x+x+x+x+x-3+x-3\,=x+x+x+x+x+x-3-3\,=6x-6$

Then add up all the sides that are in terms of $y$

$y+y+y+y+y+y+y+y$

- Collect terms and simplify

$=8y$

Add the $x$ and $y$ parts together to get the total perimeter

$6x-6+8y$

(i)

> $V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$
> 
> - where $r$ is the radius

Here you know the volume, and you want to know the radius

Start by putting the given volume into the formula in place of $V$

$381=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$

Now you need to solve that for $r$

- First multiply by 3, to get rid of the fraction on the right-hand side

$\begin{array}{ccc}3 \times 381 & = & 3 \times \frac{4}{3} pi r ^{3} \\ 1143 = & 4 pi r ^{3} \end{array}$

- Then divide both sides by $4π$, to get rid of the $4π$ on the right-hand side

$\frac{1143}{4π}=r^{3}$

**[M1]**

- You can use your calculator to work out the value of that

$r^{3}=90.957049...$

- To find the value of $r$, take the cube root of that

  - Use your calculator's memory, or the Ans key, to make sure you are taking the cube root of that exact value

$r = \sqrt[3]{90.957049...} = 4.497233...$

Round to 3 significant figures

- The fourth significant figure is a '7'

  - which tells you to round the third significant figure '9' up to a 10
  - That means put a zero where the '9' is
  
    - and increase the '4' before it by 1

**Final answer:** **4.50 cm (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $r^{3}=\frac{1143}{4π}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: For 4.497..., correctly rounded to 4.50.

parts.problemMd:
Gabriela designs the seating layout for a new theatre. 
There are three sections of seats, A, B and C.

Section A has 152 seats. 
Section B has 12.5% more seats than Section A. 
Section C has $\frac{3}{8}$ of the number of seats in Section A.

[1]

ii) Show that the total number of seats is 380.

[2]

$152\times\frac{3}{8}=57$

* ***[1]**

> *Add together the numbers of seats from sections A, B and C*

$152+171+57=380$

**380** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A car park has 880 spaces.

At 0600 one morning, $\frac{1}{40}$ of the 880 spaces are filled.

By 0630, no cars have left the car park but another $\frac{1}{5}$ of the 880 spaces are filled.

Work out the fraction of the 880 spaces that are empty at 06 30.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Multiply the amount by the fraction at 06:00 to find the number of spaces filled at that time*

$880\times\frac{1}{40}=22$

**[1]**

> *Multiply the amount by the fraction at 06:30 to find the increase in the number of spaces filled by this time*

$880\times\frac{1}{5}=176$

> *Add these values together to determine the number of spaces filled*

$22+176=198$

> *Subtract this amount from the total to determine the number of empty spaces*

$880-198=682$

**[1]**

> *Write this as a fraction of the total*

$\frac{682}{880}$ **[1]**

**Or equivalent fraction, e.g. **$\frac{31}{40}$

Insert brackets in different places and test the results

$( 9 + 4 ) - 3 \times 7 = 13 - 3 \times 7 = 13 - 21 = - 8$

$9 + 4 - ( 3 \times 7 ) = 9 + 4 - 21 = 13 - 21 = - 8$

$( 9 + 4 - 3 ) \times 7 = ( 13 - 3 ) \times 7 = 10 \times 7 = 70$

$9 + ( 4 - 3 \times 7 ) = 9 + ( 4 - 21 ) = 9 + ( - 17 ) = 9 - 17 = - 8$

parts.problemMd:
Ali rolls a fair six-sided dice labelled 1 to 6.

Let $M$ denote the event that Ali's dice lands on a number greater than 4 when rolled.

He rolls the dice twice.

![Probability tree diagram with two main branches labelled "M" and "M'" with fractions 2/3 and 2/6 leading to outcomes "M" and "M'".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/probability/set-notation-and-probability-diagrams/assets/005-probability-tree-diagram-with-two-main-branches-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> *The events are independent, rolling the dice once does not change the probability of the next*

> $M$*  and *$M'$* are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events meaning that the sum of their probabilities must be 1*

> **[exam-tip]**
> In other words, the branches at a given split must add to 1 and therefore
> 
> $\mathrm{P} ( M ) + \frac{2}{3} = 1$
$> \mathrm{P} ( M ) = 1 - \frac{2}{3}$
$> \mathrm{P} ( M ) = \frac{1}{3}$
> 
> You can also find this by counting the number of possibilities. The number can land on six numbers, two of which are greater than 4.
> 
> $\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}$

![Probability tree diagram with branches showing fractions 2/6 and 2/3, leading to nodes labelled M and M' at each split.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/probability/set-notation-and-probability-diagrams/assets/006-probability-tree-diagram-with-branches-showing-f.png)

> *Achieving the second *$M$* is also a *$\frac{1}{3}$* chance*

> *The probability of *$M$* **and** *$M$* occurring would be the product of the probabilities*

$\frac{1}{3}\times\frac{1}{3}$

**[M1]**

$\frac{1}{9}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Calculate the probability that he lands on 4 or less at least once.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The paths where at least one *$M'$* occurs are:*

$MM'\,M'M\,M'M'$

**[M1]**

> *Multiplying along the paths*

$M\timesM'=\frac{2}{9}\,M'\timesM=\frac{2}{9}\,M'\timesM'=\frac{4}{9}$

$\frac{8}{9}$

> $OB$* is a right angle with the tangent and therefore *$x$* is*

$x+33=90\,x=90-33\,x=57$

$x=57^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

> *Remember also that angles in a triangle sum to *$180^{\circ}$

$57+90+y=180\,y=180-90-57\,y=33$

$y=33^{\circ}$

$\text{sin} ( 33 ) = \frac{4}{B E}$

> *Rearrange to find *$BE$

$B E \times sin ( 33 ) = 4$
$B E = \frac{4}{ \text{sin} ( 33 ) }$
B E equals 7.3443...

**[M1]**

> *Radius is half of the diameter*

$7.3443...\div2=3.6721...$

> *Round to 3 significant figures*

$\mathrm{Area}=42.4\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

The diagram shows a circle, centre $O$, with diameter $PQ$. 
$R$ is a point on the circumference.

$PR=5.2\mathrm{cm}$, and $PR=\frac{1}{3}PQ$.
Angle $PQR=x^{\circ}$.

Give a geometrical reason why angle $PRQ$ is 90°.
parts.solutionMd:
Because $PQ$ is a diameter of the circle, angle $PRQ$ is an 'angle in a semicircle'

- By one of the circle theorems you should know, angles in a semicircle are always equal to 90°

**Final answer:** **An angle in a semicircle is 90°**

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd:
**Extract:**

The diagram shows a circle, centre O, with diameter PQ. 

R is a point on the circumference.

PR = 5.2 cm, and PR = 1/3 PQ.

Angle PQR = x°.

Angle PRQ is 90°.

Find the value of $x$.

$x=$ ..........................................
parts.solutionMd:
From part (a) you know that angle $PRQ$ is 90°

- That means triangle $PQR$ is a right-angled triangle

  - so you can use SOHCAHTOA to find $x$

The question tells you that $PR=5.2\mathrm{cm}$, and that $PR=\frac{1}{3}PQ$

- That means that the hypotenuse $PQ$ is equal to three times $PR$

$PQ=3\times5.2=15.6\mathrm{cm}$

**[B1]**

Consider the triangle $PQR$

- and label the sides H (hypotenuse), A (adjacent) and O (opposite) relative to angle $x$ (the angle at $Q$)

![Triangle PQR with right angle at R, side PR is 5.2 cm, side PQ is 15.6 cm. Angle at Q is x degrees. PQ is marked H (for hypotenuse), PR is marked O (for opposite), and QR is marked A (for adjacent).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-maths-25-core/pythagoras-and-trigonometry/trigonometry/assets/002-triangle-pqr-with-right-angle-at-r-side-pr-is-5-.png)

Here you know O and H, and you want to find the angle $x$

- so use SOH, $\mathrm{sin}=\frac{O}{H}$

  - with $O=5.2$ and $H=15.6$

$\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{5.2}{15.6}$

**[M1]**

Your calculator can work out the right-hand side

$\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{1}{3}$

- then use $\mathrm{sin}^{-1}$ on your calculator to find the value of $x$

$x = \text{sin} ^{ - } 1 ( \frac{1}{3} ) = 19.471220...$

Round to a suitable degree of accuracy

- For angles in degrees you should round to 1 decimal place (unless the question says otherwise)
- The '7' in the second decimal place says you should round the first decimal place '4' up to a 5

$x = 19.5 ( 1 \mathrm{d} . \mathrm{p} . )$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $PQ=15.6$ or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: For $\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{5.2}{15.6}$, $\mathrm{sin}x=\frac{1}{3}$ or equivalent. Earning this mark automatically earns the previous 'M' mark.
> 
> **A1**: For 19.5 or 19.47... .

| 82 | 94 | 78 | 103 | 88 | 82 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Find

ia) the mode,

.............................................. g [1]

ib)the range,

.............................................. g [1]

ic) the median.

.............................................. g [2]

ii)Another student, Toni, also brings an apple to school. The mean mass of the 7 apples is 89g.

Work out the mass of Toni’s apple.

.............................................. g [3]
parts.solutionMd:
(ia) *The most common number is 82. *

**82 g** **[1]**

(ib) *Range = largest number (103) - smallest number (78)*

> * *$103-78=25$

** ****25 g** **[1]**

(ic)*Write the numbers in order from smallest to largest.*

* **78, 82, 82, 88, 94, 103*

* ***[1]**

> *Keep crossing a number off the beginning and the end of the list to find the middle. *

$\cancel{78} , \cancel{82} , 82 , 88 , \cancel{94} , \cancel{103}$

> * The median is halfway between 82 and 88. *

**85 g** **[1]**

(ii)*Add together the 7 numbers, including Toni's apple, to work out the total weight. *

*78 + 82 + 82 + 88 + 94 + 103 + *$x$* = 527 + *$x$

* ***[1]**

> *Mean (89) = total (527 + *$x$*) *$\div$* how many pieces of data (7).*

> * *$89 = ( 527 + x ) \div 7$

> * Multiply both sides of the equation by 7.*

$\begin{gathered} 89 \\times 7 & = 527 + x \\ \\ 623 = 527 + x \end{gathered}$

* ***[1]**

> *Subtract 527 from both sides. *

$\begin{gathered} 623 - 527 & = x \\ \\ 96 = x \end{gathered}$

** ****96 g** **[1]**

> * *

parts.problemMd:
The number of examinations that each of 196 candidates takes is recorded in the table.

| Number of examinations | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of candidates | 27 | 42 | 63 | 64 |

i) Write down the range.

[1]

ii) Find the median.

[1]

iii)Calculate the mean.

[3]

iv)A candidate is selected at random. Find the probability that the candidate takes fewer than 8 examinations.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) *The range is the difference between the highest value and the lowest value *

*Highest number of examinations = 8*

*Lowest number of examinations = 5*

*8 - 5 = 3 *

**3**** ****[1]**

** **

ii)*The position of the median for an even set of data is calculated using the formula: *

> *Median position = *$\frac{n+1}{2}$

> *As *$n=196$*,*

$\frac{196+1}{2}=98.5$

> *As the data is grouped, the position of the median lies in the group that contains the 98.5*<sup>*th*</sup>* candidate in the ordered set of data*

> *Using the cumulative frequency, *

| *Number of Examinations* | *Cumulative Frequency* |
|---|---|
| *5* | *27* |
| *6* | *27 + 42 = 69* |
| *7* | *69 + 63 = 132* |
| *8* | *132 + 64 = 196* |

> *98.5 lies between 69 and 132 and so the 98.5*<sup>*th*</sup>* candidate takes 7 examinations *

**7** **[1]**

iii)*The mean is the sum of all the data points, divided by the total frequency*

> *The sum of all the data points is calculated by multiplying the number of examinations by their frequency, and adding these together*

$( 27 \times 5 ) + ( 6 \times 42 ) + ( 7 \times 63 ) + ( 8 \times 64 )$

**[1]  **

$=135+252+441+512$

$=1340$

> *Dividing the total number of examinations by the number of candidates gives us the average number of examinations per candidate*

$1340\div196=6.836734694...$

**[1]**

$6.84$ **[1]**

**An answer of **$6\frac{41}{49}$** or an answer between 6.836-6.837 will also be accepted **

iv)*To calculate the probability of an event, use the formula:*

> *The probability of an event = *$\frac{\mathrm{Number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{desired} \mathrm{outcomes}}{\mathrm{Total} \mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{outcomes}}$

*The number of desired outcomes is: *$27+42+63=132$

**[1]**

** ***The total number of outcomes is *$196$

*Place these values into the formula*

$\frac{132}{196}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
In its first 20 games of the season, a basketball team's mean score was 76.25 points per game.

In the next 12 games, the team's mean score was 80.25 points per game.

Calculate the team's mean number of points per game for all 32 of those games.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> To calculate a mean you use
> 
> $\mathrm{mean}=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{values}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{values}}$
> 
> For a question like this, that can be rearranged into the form
> 
> $\mathrm{total} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{values}=\mathrm{mean}\times\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{values}$

Find the total number of points scored in the first 20 games

$76.25\times20=1525$

**[M1]**

Find the total number of points scored in the next 12 games

$80.25\times12=963$

So the total number of points scored in the 32 games is

$1525+963=2488$

The mean number of points per game is thus

$\frac{2488}{32}=77.75$

**Final answer:** **77.75 points per game**

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: For $76.25\times20$ or $80.25\times12$ or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: For $\frac{76.25\times20+80.25\times12}{32}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: For 77.75 0160 .

parts.solutionMd:
(i) *The transformation that maps triangle **A **onto triangle **B **is a **rotation**, since the shape has been turned.   *

> *The **centre of rotation **(the point it has been turned around) is the point where the two triangles meet, *$( 2 , - 2 )$*.  *

> *It has been rotated *$90^{\circ}$* **anticlockwise** (to the right). *

** ****Rotation, centre **$(2,-2)$**, **$90^{\circ}$** anticlockwise*** ***[3]**

**one mark for each**

(ii) *The transformation that maps triangle **A** onto triangle **C **is a **translation **(since it has just been moved).  *

> *It has been translated four squares to the left and three squares up. This is written as *$\text{begin style stretchy} ( \begin{pmatrix} - 4 \\ 3\end{pmatrix} \text{stretchy} )$* as a vector.*

**Translation, **$\text{begin style stretchy} ( \begin{pmatrix} - 4 \\ 3\end{pmatrix} \text{stretchy} )$** ****[2]**

**Final answer:** **one mark for each**

(iii) *The transformation that maps triangle **A **onto triangle **D **is an **enlargement **(since the shape has changed in size). *

> *The **scale factor **is 2 (because all of the lengths of the sides have been multiplied by 2).  *

> *Draw a straight line through all the pairs of corresponding points on the original object and the enlarged image. The point of intersection of the lines is the **centre of enlargement**.  *

> *The centre of enlargement is *$( - 2 , - 5 )$*. *

** ****Enlargement, scale factor 2, centre**$(-2,-5)$*  ***[3]**

**one mark for each**
